standard.title: Post-War World Events and Their Effects on Australia
standard.description: the effects of significant post–Second World War world events, ideas and developments on Australian society
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have studied significant post-WWI events and their effects on Australia, including the interwar period, the Great Depression, and the rise of totalitarian regimes.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse the effects of significant post-WWII world events, ideas and developments on Australian society, including the waves of migration driven by post-war global conditions.

nodes.label: Post-war conditions driving migration
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse the causes and conditions that led to increased migration to Australia after WWII, including the role of specific world events in changing public opinion and government policy.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two post-war world events or conditions that drove migration to Australia and explain how each influenced Australian government policy.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse the causes of increased post-war migration: the Holocaust and the plight of refugees in war-ravaged Europe changing public opinion; the 'populate or perish' strategic imperative; the White Australia Policy as a framework shaping who was accepted; the Displaced Persons program bringing European migrants; explain the push factors (war, persecution, economic devastation) and pull factors (Australia's stability, economic opportunity, government recruitment) driving migration.
wider: Investigate the Displaced Persons (DP) migration program of the late 1940s in depth, examining the screening processes, the conditions migrants came from, and the reception they received in Australia

Examine how the Holocaust specifically changed Australian and international attitudes to refugees — tracing how the mass murder of European Jews became public knowledge and how this knowledge shaped post-war refugee policy
nodes.hinge_reason: The post-war conditions and policy framework established here underpin K08 (changing perspectives on migration). Students who do not understand the 'populate or perish' logic and the White Australia Policy context cannot make sense of why attitudes to migration changed across the 1950s–1980s.

response_modes.reason: Explicitly teach the push/pull factor framework as an analytical tool — students should be able to categorise and explain migration drivers systematically before applying it to specific migration waves.

success_criteria: Identify at least two causes of increased migration to Australia after WWII and explain each
Explain the 'populate or perish' policy and what it reveals about post-war Australian strategic thinking
Use the push/pull factor framework to explain why a specific group migrated to Australia after WWII

nodes.label: Waves of migration — patterns and origins
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate the nature of successive waves of migration to Australia from the 1950s to the 2000s, explaining the origins of each wave and the push and pull factors driving it.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least two distinct waves of migration to Australia since WWII, identifying the countries of origin and the push and pull factors for each.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate the nature and scale of successive migration waves: Europe 1950s–1960s (Displaced Persons, '£10 Poms', southern Europeans); Asia 1970s–2000s (Vietnamese refugees, then broader Asian migration); Middle East 1980s–1990s; India 1990s–2000s; Africa 2000s; for each wave, explain the push factors (war, persecution, economic hardship) and pull factors (Australia's stability, immigration programs, economic opportunity); describe how the numbers and origins of migrants changed across decades.
wider: Investigate one specific migration wave in depth through personal accounts and oral histories — examining the gap between official policy narratives and individual migrant experiences
Analyse demographic data on migration waves using graphs, examining what the data reveals about how Australia's population composition changed across the second half of the 20th century

response_modes.reason: Students need a working knowledge of the sequence and origins of migration waves as a foundation for K08's analysis of changing attitudes. A structured timeline with key wave characteristics (origin, push factors, numbers, policy context) builds this repertoire.

success_criteria: Describe at least two distinct waves of post-war migration to Australia, identifying countries of origin and time period
Apply the push/pull factor framework to explain why each identified wave occurred
Describe how the origins of migrants to Australia changed across the second half of the 20th century
